title: Fooling Some of the People All of the Time: A Long Short Story, Updated with New Epilogue
author: David Einhorn
summary:
*Fooling Some of the People All of the Time* is hedge fund manager David Einhorn's first-person account of his six-year public battle with Allied Capital, a publicly traded business development company he and his firm, Greenlight Capital, publicly identified as a short-sale candidate in 2002 due to what he came to believe was aggressive, misleading accounting used to overstate the value of its loan portfolio and mask underlying losses. What began as a single investment thesis presented at a charity investing conference (the Sohn Conference) escalated into a prolonged, multi-front conflict involving Allied's aggressive countermeasures against Einhorn personally, extensive but ultimately slow-moving regulatory scrutiny, and years of public dispute over whose numbers — Einhorn's or Allied's — actually reflected reality.

The book's early sections establish Einhorn's investment philosophy and process, walking through how Greenlight Capital typically evaluates a potential short position by examining the true underlying economics of a business, comparing that reality to reported earnings, and assessing whether the incentives of company decision-makers are actually aligned with outside investors — a framework Einhorn presents as standard value-investing analysis applied specifically to identify overvalued or fraudulent companies rather than undervalued ones. Applying this framework to Allied Capital, Einhorn concluded the company was systematically overvaluing distressed loans in its portfolio to avoid recognizing losses that would have hurt its stock price and its ability to raise capital.

The middle sections of the book detail the escalating conflict that followed Einhorn's public short thesis: Allied's management aggressively challenged Einhorn's credibility, allegedly pursued his personal phone records, and lobbied regulators and lawmakers, while government agencies including the SEC, the Small Business Administration, and eventually the FBI became involved in investigations that, in Einhorn's account, moved with striking slowness and, at points, seemed to focus more on scrutinizing the short-sellers raising concerns than on the underlying allegations of accounting fraud itself. Einhorn documents specific instances of what he characterizes as regulatory failure — examinations that dragged on for years without conclusive action, and a broader pattern of institutional reluctance to challenge a company with political connections and lobbying resources.

The book closes with an epilogue, added for the updated edition, addressing Allied Capital's eventual dramatic decline and 2010 acquisition by Ares Capital at a steep discount to its former valuation — a resolution that arrived only after this book's original 2008 publication, and which Einhorn presents as ultimate, if very delayed, vindication of the original short thesis. Beyond the specific Allied Capital narrative, Einhorn uses the book to argue more broadly for the social and market value of public short-selling and open critical debate about company accounting, positioning aggressive, well-researched skepticism — even when it makes a company's management furious — as a check on corporate fraud that formal regulatory processes alone often fail to provide in a timely way.

sections.title: The Sohn Conference and the Initial Thesis
sections.summary:
This opening part introduces Einhorn's investment background and process, then walks through the 2002 charity investing conference where he first publicly presented Allied Capital as a short-sale candidate, laying out his early analysis of the company's loan accounting practices.
Einhorn explains his standard framework for evaluating a potential investment — examining a business's true underlying economics, comparing that reality to its reported earnings, and assessing whether management's incentives align with outside shareholders — and shows how applying that framework to Allied Capital surfaced specific accounting red flags around how the company valued distressed loans in its portfolio.
The part closes with the immediate aftermath of the presentation: Allied's management publicly and aggressively disputed Einhorn's analysis, setting the stage for the multi-year conflict the rest of the book documents.
keyLessons: Einhorn's short thesis relied on comparing a company's true underlying economics to its reported earnings, not just skepticism alone.
Assessing management incentive alignment with shareholders is treated as a core part of investment analysis.
A single public presentation can trigger a prolonged, high-stakes conflict when it directly challenges a company's public narrative.

sections.title: Allied's Countermeasures
sections.summary:
This part details the aggressive response from Allied Capital's management following Einhorn's public short thesis, including efforts to challenge his credibility, allegations involving his personal phone records, and lobbying directed at regulators and lawmakers.
Einhorn documents specific episodes of this conflict in granular, forensic detail, presenting internal communications, regulatory filings, and correspondence to substantiate his account of the pressure campaign against him and his firm.
The part closes by framing this response as, in Einhorn's view, itself a form of evidence — a company confident in the accuracy of its accounting, he argues, would engage with the substance of the criticism rather than focus its energy on discrediting the critic.
keyLessons: Allied's response focused heavily on challenging Einhorn's credibility rather than directly engaging with the accounting substance.
Einhorn treats the intensity of a company's counterattack against a critic as itself potentially informative.
The conflict extended well beyond investment analysis into personal and legal territory.

sections.title: Regulatory Failure and Institutional Slowness
sections.summary:
This part examines the multi-year involvement of government agencies — the SEC, the Small Business Administration, the Department of Justice, and eventually the FBI — in investigating both Allied Capital's accounting and, at points, Einhorn and other short-sellers who had raised concerns about the company.
Einhorn presents this as a case study in institutional dysfunction: examinations that dragged on for years without conclusive resolution, regulatory attention that he argues was at points misdirected toward scrutinizing critics rather than the underlying allegations, and a broader pattern where a well-resourced, politically connected company was able to slow accountability considerably.
The part closes by connecting this specific case to a broader argument about the market's need for independent, public critical analysis (like well-researched short-selling) as a supplement to regulatory oversight, given how slowly formal institutional processes moved in this instance.
keyLessons: Regulatory investigations into the underlying allegations moved slowly over multiple years without swift resolution.
Einhorn argues attention was at points misdirected toward scrutinizing critics rather than the company's accounting.
The case is presented as evidence for the value of independent, public critical analysis as a supplement to formal regulatory oversight.

sections.title: Epilogue: Vindication, Delayed
sections.summary:
Added for the updated edition, this closing part addresses Allied Capital's eventual sharp decline and its 2010 acquisition by Ares Capital at a steep discount to its former valuation — a resolution occurring after the book's original 2008 publication.
Einhorn presents this outcome as vindication of his original 2002 short thesis, while also reflecting on how long that vindication took to arrive and what that delay itself suggests about the pace of accountability in public markets when a company actively resists scrutiny.
The part, and the book, close by returning to Einhorn's broader argument: aggressive, well-researched public skepticism about company accounting serves an important market function, since formal regulatory processes alone, in this case, took years longer than a careful independent analysis to reach the same underlying conclusion.
keyLessons: Allied Capital's 2010 acquisition by Ares Capital at a steep discount is presented as delayed vindication of Einhorn's original thesis.
The multi-year gap between the original thesis and its eventual vindication is treated as evidence of how slowly market accountability can move.
The book's closing argument favors robust, public short-seller research as a valuable check alongside formal regulatory oversight.
Evaluate a company's true underlying economics against its reported earnings, not just the headline numbers.
Assess whether company management's incentives are actually aligned with outside shareholders before trusting reported results.
Be prepared for aggressive resistance when publicly challenging a company's accounting, separate from the merits of the analysis itself.
Treat a company's response to criticism — engaging with substance versus attacking the critic — as potentially informative in itself.
Understand that regulatory processes can move far more slowly than independent, well-researched public analysis.
Recognize that public short-selling research, done rigorously, can serve a market accountability function regulators don't always fill quickly.
Expect that being right about a thesis and having the market validate it can be separated by years.
Document analysis and communications carefully, since a drawn-out public dispute may require substantiating a position long after it was first made.

quotes.text: There were three basic questions to resolve: First, what are the true economics of the business?
This is a long story about a long short.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Einhorn's Three Basic Investment Questions
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Greenlight Capital's core evaluative framework: first, what are the true economics of the business; second, how do those economics compare to the company's reported earnings; and third, how are the interests of company decision-makers aligned with the interests of outside investors. Einhorn presents this as standard value-investing analysis, applicable to identifying both undervalued and overvalued/fraudulent companies.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: The Sohn Conference and the Initial Thesis

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Short Thesis as Public Accountability
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Einhorn's broader argument that well-researched, publicly presented short-selling serves a market accountability function — surfacing accounting problems and misaligned incentives — that can act faster and more effectively than formal regulatory processes, particularly against companies with resources and political connections to slow institutional scrutiny.

actionSteps: When evaluating any investment (long or short), explicitly write out the company's true underlying economics separately from its reported earnings, and compare the two directly before forming a conclusion.
Before trusting a company's reported results, research whether management's compensation and incentive structures are actually aligned with outside shareholder interests.
If you're researching a public company skeptically, document your sources and reasoning as you go, since a drawn-out public dispute may require substantiating your position much later.
Practice separating the substance of a critique from a company's response to it — notice whether pushback engages with specific facts or focuses on discrediting the critic.
reflectionQuestions: How much of your own investment or business decision-making relies on reported headline numbers versus a direct comparison to underlying economic reality?
How do you personally weigh the discomfort of publicly disagreeing with a consensus or an authority against the value of raising a well-researched concern?

points: The book is written entirely from Einhorn's own first-person perspective as the central figure in the dispute, and while he includes documentary evidence to substantiate his account, readers should recognize it's an advocacy narrative for his own position rather than a neutral third-party investigation.

Some readers and reviewers have noted that portions of the book, particularly around the regulatory and legal minutiae of the multi-year dispute, require a level of forensic accounting and legal detail that can be dense and slow-moving compared to a more conventional business narrative.

Although Allied Capital's eventual 2010 acquisition at a steep discount is widely treated as broadly consistent with Einhorn's original skepticism, the book itself, as an advocacy account, does not deeply engage with counterarguments that might complicate a fully one-sided reading of the outcome.

The book's broader argument for the social value of short-selling is a longstanding, genuinely contested position in finance and policy circles — critics of short-selling argue it can also be used to spread damaging misinformation about fundamentally sound companies, a risk the book, understandably, spends little time examining given its focus on defending Einhorn's own specific, ultimately vindicated case.
criticalTake.contextNote: Allied Capital was acquired by Ares Capital Corporation in 2010 at a price well below its earlier peak valuation, an outcome that occurred after the book's original 2008 publication and is addressed directly in the updated edition's epilogue.

whoThisIsFor: Readers interested in hedge fund investing, short-selling, forensic accounting analysis, or detailed real-world case studies of conflict between an activist investor and a public company's management and regulators.
whenToReadThis: Best read by readers with some existing familiarity with basic accounting and public market mechanics, given the book's detailed, sometimes dense forensic material.

authorBio.name: David Einhorn
authorBio.bio:
David Einhorn is an American hedge fund manager and founder of Greenlight Capital, a firm he built around a value-investing approach applied to both long and short positions, with the Allied Capital case becoming one of his most widely known public short theses.

Einhorn built a reputation in investing circles for detailed, research-intensive public presentations of investment theses, including his high-profile 2002 Sohn Conference presentation on Allied Capital that forms the starting point of this book's narrative, as well as later prominent public positions on other companies.

Beyond his Allied Capital case, Einhorn has remained an active, publicly visible hedge fund manager and occasional poker player, known within the investing community for a research-driven, contrarian, and willing-to-be-publicly-controversial approach to both long and short investment theses.
